column41: Two left dentaries were found with other regurgitated eagle pellet material below the Rob Roy WTE nest by raptor PhD student Esteban Fuentes. They were found a few days after the 2003 bush fire.  One dentary still retained red muscle fibres.  Both are now in the ANWC collection.  At that time there were no captive collections of Bandicoots in the ACT, because the former CSIRO collection of I. macroura had long gone, as had the Mugga Lane Zoo.   And the Tidbinbilla collection of I. obesulus had not commenced.  So these two animals came from a wild population. Initially some confusion arose because the eagle nest location had been falsified to protect it.  The nest location given here is closer to the real 'Rob Roy WTE nest' but still only approximately correct.  This is not important because the nest location is not likely to be where the bandicoots were predated by the eagles!  That place remains unknown.

column41: As of this week the St Helens Biolink Project has gained a very powerful ally. No, not a top funder nor a international environmental advocate. Even better. This week we gained the support of the very animal we have been protecting with fox and feral cat control.Ok, that all sounds a bit obtuse I agree - but humour me. What I mean is that after four years of fortnightly treks out to St Helens to check our remote sensing cameras that look for foxes/cats/bandicoots - yesterday I managed to make a film showing the bandicoot we have worked so hard to save. And it wandered up to me as if I was part of the scenery.....well, perhaps after four years I am really.So, if you have never seen a local Southern Brown Bandicoot in action - it's time you did. This little population of Bandicoots at St Helens is the only known in the Moyne/Warrnambool Region. Once upon a time they were as common as rabbits, and many of the older farmers recall them being caught when rabbiting. Things have changed for the worse with foxes and cats and habitat loss - but at St Helens we and our project partners (which include some of those old farmers), have managed to make a difference for this little animal - and I would love everyone who cares about this kind of thing to feel the same sense of Wow about that achievement that we do.I have posted the video on YouTube and the link to it is here: https://youtu.be/kYmdxv0hOxkPlease share it with anyone you think might enjoy this too.CheersLisette

column41: The Basalt to Bay Landcare Network received funding from Pacific Hydro Sustainable Communities Fund to conduct a fauna camera survey of the St Helens Reserve (Parks Victoria) in Nove/Dec 2012. These images come from that survey and are verification that a small population of Southern Brown Bandicoot persists at St Helens. From these results, future planning with the St Helens Landcare Group is occuring to link this reserve to other locations both north and south, including a biodiversity corridor to Pallisters Reserve on Masons Rd. This Trust for Nature Property is a key remnant in the St Helens/Orford region. Surveying of the by the Framlingham Aboriginal Trust on their Property at Deen Maar is also occuring to provide better data on the fauna values of the wider landscape of the Kanawinka Region. All enquiries about these images to The Basalt to Bay Landcare Network  basalttobay@gmail.com

column41: Just wanted to let you know that I have a small population of Southern brown bandicoots at my place at 95 Lakeside Drive Conjola Park. Just recently (as in the past 4-6 months) arrived in my back yard. I wanted to record the sightings for you. I have a patch of low vegetation which they seem to like plus post bushfire, the bushland between my place & the lake – some 50-75 metres wide, Is quite thick with low undergrowth post bushfires (I’ve refused to let anyone clear it) so there is quite good, if relatively small habitat for them. Unfortunately they’ve found ways to get into my house at night, so I’ve been able to meet them face to face. (I have to work out how they are getting in!!)
